Hidden by the tree: a cell with no opening copies the opening of the same column on the nearest floor; on a floor where the other bays have balconies, the hidden bay gets one too. Both are marked inferred (light grey-blue in Rhino, hatched in the drawing).
Redrawn in rhino/NOMAD.3dm on the same layer ('06 NOMAD experiments::facade Av Diagonal 413'); backup first.
experiments.result: Floors at 0, 6.27, 10.17, 13.98, 18.09, 22.99, 26.01 m (floor 5 moved from 22.05 to 22.99 once its balconies were found). 47 openings: ground 4 shopfronts + 1 door; floor 1 five bay windows; floors 2-5 five balcony doors each with their balconies (floor 5: four curved stone balconies found, one inferred behind the palm); top floor 4 windows (one inferred). 6 columns.
learned: The curved stone balconies were found once each bay was asked on its own; a whole-facade question missed them.
A box that includes the stone arch under a balcony is still a balcony: only its bottom is used.
The roof parapet and the top rail of a lower balcony look like balconies: the position rules (lowest third, nearest floor line, no attic balconies) remove them.
experiments.decision: Keep: tree mask, bay-by-bay check, grid snapping, inferred openings marked. Next: corner buildings (two facade planes) and speed, then the city.

experiments.title: Floor heights measured at the facade, and the facade rules
experiments.question: The heights of Av. Diagonal 413 did not look right. Where does each floor's height come from, and what rules make a facade drawing read like the building?
did: LiDAR measured where the facade is (src/facade/heights.py): street level on the pavement strip 1-4 m in front of the facade line; facade height = median top in the strip 0,5-2,5 m behind it (the front wall's top, the cornice). The old method used ground within 25 m and the 75th percentile of the whole roof.

Edges: of the long vertical lines either side, the pair that makes the Catastro street front fit the LiDAR height scale (outer side of the corner pilasters). Detection stays on the same crop as before, so the boxes do not change; only the measuring does.

Floor lines must sit above the heads of the floor below + 0,30 m (our assumption). Then the user's rule: the ground floor has its own height and every floor above has one same height, fitted by least squares; the rest up to the cornice is the cornice band.

Drawing rules: one opening width and height on the typical floors; one size for the ground-floor arches (shopfronts and entrance); symmetry tested (60 % of openings with a mirror partner within 0,8 m), not assumed; missing balconies stamped by repetition; everything inferred marked.

Rules searched in our rulebook: only minimum clear heights (Decret 141/2012 2,40 m for converted premises; MPGM 1999 art. 225 2,50 m below and above a mezzanine). The PGM floor heights for planta baixa / plantes pis are not in the rulebook.
The method is written down in docs/facade_workflow.md.
experiments.result: Street level 48,34 m (pavement, spread 0,19 m; was 48,10). Facade height to the cornice 30,47 m; pediment 34,1 m; corners about 32,7 m. The old 32,8 m was the corner ornaments: every floor was about 8 % too tall. Edges moved 1 m out on the left; across and up scales now 27,0 and 27,3 px/m (within 1,5 %). Floors: ground 5,76 m (clear 5,46), floors 1-6 3,79 m each (clear 3,49), cornice band 1,96 m; measured lines within 0,34 m of the rule except floor 5 (+0,53 m, on the deep carved band). Typical openings 1,58 x 2,99 m; ground arches 2,97 m wide, top 4,35 m. Symmetry test: 20 of 27 openings have a partner.
learned: A whole-plot roof height mixes the cornice with ornaments, huts and back parts: measure at the facade.
Two independent measures (Catastro width, LiDAR height) placed the true edges: the strongest vertical line was the inner side of a pilaster.
Measured floor heights one by one all differ; the building's rule (ground floor + equal floors) fits them within about 0,3 m and reads right.
experiments.decision: docs/facade_workflow.md is the method for every facade. The site's height box will take the ground floor's clear height from the facade when one has been read. Next: floor plans.

experiments.title: Shop shapes cut to their true size; doors, entrances and the census and land registry facts
experiments.question: Our shop shape was the building's whole ground floor, often much bigger than the premises. Can the land registry's unit sizes and the city census doors give each premises a truer shape, and what else can the app tell about each shop and its building?
did: Rule A (one shop unit on the ground floor): when the shape is more than 15 % bigger than the unit, keep the part behind the door on its street facade (narrower and centred on the door when the front is long), as deep as the unit's m2 (src/building/cut_shells.py).

Rule B (2 or more shop units): the street front is shared out between the premises doors of the 2024 city census (halfway to the next door); the area stays between the smallest and largest unit; shallower than 4 m -> narrowed round the door.

Cuts narrower than 2,5 m, doors more than 8 m from the building or cuts that lose the street facade keep the footprint. Every cut is labelled 'assumed (rule A/B)' in the app; the premises' own Catastro unit plan still comes first.

Building entrances: Catastro INSPIRE Addresses for Barcelona (3,7 MB), points marked 'Entrance', matched by cadastral reference (src/building/entrances.py). Shop doors: every premises of the building in the census, empty or in use.

Facts for the app (src/building/site_facts.py, site/data/facts/): census status and offer, where the premises opens (street, market, gallery, shopping centre, shopping street), night / 24 h flags, the other premises in the building and their activity; land registry year built, floors, every unit with use and m2.
The 1:1000 city map (CartoBCN TOPO1000 GPKG, Dec 2025) downloaded: the old 652 MB file never finished because the server drops every connection after about 6 minutes.
experiments.result: 2,932 of 6,056 premises now have a cut shape: 498 by rule A, 2,459 by rule B (2,261 have no shop unit on the ground floor and keep the footprint). 3,479 of 5,322 modelled buildings have a registered entrance; 13,833 shop doors. Viladomat 147 (rule A, 121 m2): 5 layouts, 1 home each, 32 s in the browser.
learned: The land registry's unit size is the best single check on a shape; the footprint over-promised homes in shared ground floors.
Census door points place each premises along its street front, so a shared ground floor can be split without a plan.
Land registry addresses mark the building's door ('Entrance'): the existing stair can be placed from it where there is no plan.
experiments.decision: Cut shapes are used in Design homes after the premises' own Catastro plan and before the footprint, always labelled assumed. Next: checklist item 6 (stair and entrance from the address point and light wells), and the 1:1000 map's facade and party-wall lines.
figures: Sample cut shapes: grey = the building's ground floor, orange = the premises after rule A (top) or rule B (bottom), blue = street facade, star = the census door.

experiments.title: Conversion group (Decret 141/2012 Annex 4) for each shop
experiments.question: Which rules apply when a shop becomes homes depends on the shop's share of the building (Annex 4 Grup C or D). Does the team's new group file change NOMAD's answers?
did: The team's annex4_grup.json (tools/annex4_grup.py, from the Catastro CAT file: the shop's built area / the building's) copied into the local site.
Find your shop and Design homes show each shop's group, its share and what it means in plain words.

The engine (src/app/nomad_web.py) puts a 'Conversion group' card first on every layout; for Grup D with 8 homes or more it checks the community room (Annex 1 2.6: 1,20 x 0,80 m, +0,05 m2 per home over 12) against the plan's shared rooms, and a fail turns YES into PARTLY.
Grup D's other building rules do not bite on one ground floor: every home is on the entry level (2.1 route met), no lift (2.2.2 landing), and NOMAD's shop plans light no room from a patio (2.5.1).
experiments.result: Groups: 5,094 Grup C, 151 Grup D, 60 Grup B, 767 not known (NOMAD applies Grup C to these). The generator already followed Grup C, so most answers do not change. París 95 (Grup D, 64,3 %): layouts as before, group card shown.
learned: Most empty shops are a small part of their building (Grup C): the building rules (stairs, lift, patios) are exempt, which NOMAD already assumed.
Grup D adds little on one ground floor; the community room matters only from 8 homes.
experiments.decision: Group shown and checked locally; nothing pushed. Grup B shops (60) could go to the whole-building mode next.

experiments.title: The building's hall and stair where there is no plan (rule C)
experiments.question: Most buildings have no plan of their entrance hall and stair, so NOMAD could draw homes over them. Can open data place them well enough?
did: Tested on the buildings whose real hall and stair are known (Catastro plans we hold, private calibration only).
Sizes: the median of 1,692 real halls with their stairs is 3,5 x 7,6 m (p10-p90 1,4-8,5 m wide).

Three ways to place it from the land registry entrance point: a straight box in from the door; a hall from the door to the nearest light well with the stair beside it; a hall from the door to the stair tower (the building's smallest part as tall as its tallest, INSPIRE building parts).

Rule C uses the stair tower first, then the light well, then the box; marked 'assumed' with its tested accuracy; the generator keeps homes off it and may use it as the flats' way in (src/building/shop_data.py step 2b, site/data/cores.json).

Looked for better data: the CAT file lists a ground-floor common area for only 25 of 5,322 buildings (it records common parts for the whole building); the 1:1000 map draws no stairs inside buildings; the stair tower in the INSPIRE parts was the useful find.
experiments.result: Lands on the real hall/stair: door-to-tower 93 % (171 buildings), door-to-well 91 % (88), box 72 % (294). The stair tower exists in 52 % of buildings and touches the real hall/stair in 87 %; the stair touches a light well in 89 % of buildings that have one. 2,942 buildings get an assumed hall (655 tower, 1,285 light well, 1,002 box). Muntaner 336 and Creu dels Molers 12: layouts as before, homes kept off the hall.
learned: The place is right far more often than the outline: about a third of the guess is real hall or stair.
The stair tower above the roof is the best open signal for where the stair is.
One size for every hall is the weak part; real halls range from 1,4 to 8,5 m wide.
experiments.decision: Rule C in the app, labelled with its method and accuracy. Backlog: size each hall per building (no open source found yet; real plans from the Arxiu / COAC would replace it).

experiments.title: Second facade: Pl. Sortidor 4 (narrow, 6 floors)
experiments.question: Does the facade method from Av. Diagonal 413 work on a different building: narrow, three columns, a pair of narrow windows in the middle?
did: Ran src/facade/facade.py steps 1-4 on Pl. Sortidor 4 (0006311DF3800E). Straightening worked first time.

Fixes found on the way, each checked to leave Diagonal 413 unchanged: the main piece of the footprint (not the first, a 3 m sliver); street level only from doors and shopfronts in the lowest fifth of the photo (a 'shopfront' at first-floor height had set the street 4,5 m too high); search the whole facade again when the strongest lines cut part of it off (the left balcony column was never searched); symmetry also needs the mirror line within 8 % of the width from the middle; a 'balcony' under 0,6 m is a ledge; columns of narrow windows keep their own width; balconies stamped only in columns that have them on most floors.
experiments.result: Ground floor 4,57 m, upper floors 3,16 m each (measured lines within 0,37 m of the fit); width 8,6 m (Catastro) fits the LiDAR scale exactly; symmetrical about 4,25 m (middle 4,28 m); ground floor right (shop, entrance door, restaurant door). learned: The method carries over, but each new facade showed a new way to fail: the fixes are general rules, not tuning for one building.
Detection is the weak step on narrow facades: one box over two windows, ledges read as balconies.
experiments.decision: Show the user; next fixes if wanted: split a box that covers two narrower openings seen on other floors; copy balconies to the mirrored column on symmetrical facades.

experiments.title: Analyse the facade before drawing it: repeated floors, typical floor, inventory
experiments.question: Reading each floor on its own made one floor differ from the others by mistake (a pair read as one window, missing balconies). Can NOMAD first find which floors repeat and read the typical floor once?
did: New step 3b in src/facade/facade.py: level the leftover perspective, compare the floors' bands (lined up first), blend the repeated floors into one clean typical floor, vote across floors, read it as an architect (balcony = door behind it, pier = two windows, railing is not a window), write an inventory, then draw every floor from its type.
Run on Pl. Sortidor 4; Diagonal 413 has no inventory and keeps its approved drawing.
experiments.result: Sortidor 4: floors 1-5 found to be one type (similarity 0,45-0,77 after lining up); typical floor = balcony 1,74 m + door 1,00 x 2,50 m | two windows 0,58 and 0,63 m (sill 0,82, head 2,50) | balcony 1,53 m + door 1,00 m; ground = shop window 2,43 x 3,44 m, entrance door 1,07 m, restaurant door 1,67 m. All floors now drawn alike. The leftover tilt was 14 deg at the very top of the photo (the left balconies stood 55 px higher than the right).
learned: Repetition is the strongest clue on a facade: read the typical floor once, from all floors together.
Rules an architect uses (a balcony has a door) fill what the detector misses.
experiments.decision: Waiting for the user's approval before Sortidor 4 goes to the app. Floor heights that change upwards are a next refinement.
